content: All clinics provide a comprehensive package for HIV prevention and treatment, as well as cervical cancer screening services. Community members are actively involved in deciding the locations of service sites, ensuring discretion and acceptability. Outreach teams work in coordination with peer support teams to implement activities effectively. The program offers free services, including behavioral, biomedical, and structural interventions, adhering to national guidelines. Regular training sessions and performance reviews for peer leaders are conducted to maintain high-quality services. In Kenya, where sex work is illegal, partnerships with other organizations and government agencies working with key populations are essential. In 2013, outreach activities by SWOP (Sex Workers Outreach Program) resulted in 103,000 contacts with sex workers, and 31,000 HIV tests were conducted. Strong peer networks and data sharing between clinics via a virtual private network (VPN) help address challenges related to the mobility of sex workers. SWOP has played a key role in establishing clinical guidelines for syndromic STI treatment, which is now part of the NASCOP health policy. However, male sex workers who have sex with men face dual stigma, hostility, and persecution, with an HIV incidence rate of 9 per 100 person-years. SWOP collaborates with NASCOP and other stakeholders to address their specific needs. Retention of trained peer educators is another challenge, as many move to other programs, necessitating constant retraining. The AIDS Myanmar Association (AMA) is a network of over 2,000 female, male, and transgender sex workers. The program focuses on capacity building and community mobilization to advocate for the health and human rights of sex workers. AMA employs innovative outreach methods to reach young sex workers, providing peer support and access to health information and services. Outreach workers are trained to be sensitive to the needs of young people and do not request identifying information. They distribute STI and HIV prevention tools, link individuals to sex worker-friendly health facilities, and provide follow-up counseling and care for those living with HIV. AMA also supports imprisoned sex workers, particularly young individuals abandoned by their families, by providing nutritional support. The River of Life (ROLi) program in the Philippines focuses on HIV risk reduction among adolescent males who have sex with men. It uses self-assessment toolkits, workshops, and peer group work to help participants assess and reduce risky behaviors. The program serves 6,000 young people, mostly males aged 13–17, many of whom are out of school, live in poverty, sell sex, and use drugs. Outreach is conducted through peer-to-peer interactions, both in-person and online, and participants can join moderated Facebook groups for discussions about behavior change. The program has been adapted to serve other key populations, including female sex workers and young people who inject drugs. In South Africa, the Re-Action. program, in collaboration with the Department of Health, aims to reduce new HIV infections among female sex workers and their clients in rural Mpumalanga Province. The program also addresses vulnerabilities such as violence, exploitation, substance abuse, and social exclusion through life skills mentoring and community sensitization. A mobile clinic provides free services, including health risk screening, HIV testing and treatment, and referrals. Outreach workers assist clients who default on treatment and ensure confidentiality by assigning workers from outside the clients' communities. The program has reached approximately 4,100 female sex workers, with increased awareness of legal rights and support services. In San Francisco, USA, St. James Infirmary is a peer-led clinic run by and for current and former sex workers. It offers free, confidential, and non-judgmental medical and social services, including primary care, HIV and STI testing, hormone therapy, acupuncture, massage, support groups, needle exchange, and naloxone training. The clinic operates on harm reduction principles, creating a welcoming environment for sex workers to access care without fear of stigma. Outreach is conducted at strip clubs, massage parlors, and on the streets. Since 1999, over 3,500 clients have accessed care, with an additional 30,000 contacts made through outreach. In Zimbabwe, the Sisters with a Voice program, run by CeSHHAR, provides integrated services for sex workers across 36 sites. The program offers HIV testing and counseling, syndromic STI treatment, contraceptives, health education, and legal advice. Cervical cancer screening is being rolled out, with nurses trained in visual inspection and cryotherapy. Peer educators conduct community mobilization sessions on topics such as self-worth, behavior change, contraception, and advocacy. By 2013, the program had served over 14,000 women, with significant increases in HIV testing and ART uptake among participants. The Silueta X Association in Ecuador promotes health among young transgender individuals and addresses risks associated with non-professional feminizing hormone regimens. The program uses peer communication and social networks to reach participants and educate them about safe hormone use. Despite funding challenges, the association continues to incorporate this information into its HIV prevention training and social events. In New York City, the Health Outreach to Teens (HOTT) program serves LGBTQ adolescents, homeless youth, and those living with HIV. It provides acute and primary care, mental health services, HIV testing, case management, and health education. The program creates a trans-affirming environment and offers rapid access to appointments, engaging youth who face significant psychosocial stressors.
